items.title: Comparative advantage is about relative, not absolute, costs
items.claim: Ricardo's 1817 numerical example: Portugal can produce both wine and cloth more efficiently than England (absolute advantage in both). According to comparative advantage, should both countries still trade?

options.text: Yes — both countries benefit from specialising in the good in which they have the lowest opportunity cost. Portugal specialises in wine (relative advantage); England in cloth
Only one country benefits from trade

items.reveal:
Ricardo's 'Principles of Political Economy' (1817) used Portugal-England wine-cloth as a thought experiment, not necessarily descriptive of the actual trade. The insight: even if one country is more productive in everything, gains from trade still arise from differences in relative productivity.

Real-world caveats: factor mobility within countries is imperfect; adjustment costs (displaced workers) can be substantial; gains can be uneven across groups; political economy of trade (David Autor's 'China shock' research on US manufacturing) shows specific losers as well as aggregate gains.
items.why: Comparative advantage is foundational but often taught without the adjustment cost and distributional caveats that determine whether trade liberalisation is politically sustainable.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.

items.title: Acemoglu and Robinson argue institutions explain development
items.claim: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's 2001 AER paper used settler mortality as an instrument for institutional quality. What did they find?

options.text: Places where European settlement was deadly (tropics) developed 'extractive' colonial institutions; places suitable for settlement got 'inclusive' institutions. Institutional differences persist and explain a large share of cross-country income variation today

items.reveal:
The 2001 AER paper used settler mortality data to instrument for current institutions (since geography affects mortality but, AJR argue, only affects current outcomes through institutions). Their book 'Why Nations Fail' (2012) developed the inclusive vs extractive institutions framework for a general audience.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson won the 2024 Nobel for this body of work. Critics (Glaeser, Sachs) have argued for the role of geography, human capital and culture; the debate over weights between institutional and other factors continues.
items.why: Cross-country growth differences are large and persistent. Identifying causal drivers is genuinely difficult; AJR's instrumental approach was an influential attempt.
